1:
Every voice begins by denying that the passage commands anything. Henry says it is the permission the Pharisees erroneously cited as a precept when they told our Saviour that Moses commanded a writing of divorcement; he suffered it only because of the hardness of their hearts, lest men without that liberty should rule their wives with rigour. Wesley states the same in three terms, that it is not a command, nor an allowance and approbation, but merely a permission for the prevention of greater mischiefs, and that only until the time of reformation. Calvin goes furthest, that divorce was never in accordance with the Law at all, being repugnant to the first institution of God: the bond between husband and wife was declared closer than that between parent and child, so that if a son cannot shake off the paternal yoke no cause can dissolve a marriage. He allows only that God chose to make some provision for women who were cruelly oppressed. Henry adds that divorce was in use before this, being taken for granted in Leviticus, so that Moses gave rules for an existing practice.

What the uncleanness is that grounds the permission divides them sharply. Henry holds it must be less than adultery, since for that the woman was to die, and less than the suspicion of it, since for that there were the waters of jealousy; but it must be something, for it was not enough that a man did not like his wife, and he had to show a cause that made her disagreeable to him though it might not make her so to another. Clarke takes the opposite view and rests it on practice rather than the word: any cause of dislike will do, since it is certain a Jew might put away his wife for any cause that seemed good to him. Wesley stands between, allowing a distemper of body or quality of mind not observed before marriage, or some light carriage, but nothing amounting to adultery.

Keil explains the instrument. The Hebrew term means a hewing or cutting off from the man with whom the wife was to be one flesh, and he thinks the custom was adopted in Egypt, where writing had already found its way into all the relations of life. His substantial point concerns the fourth verse: since Moses could not abolish the custom outright, the law that a first husband might never take his divorced wife back once she had married another, even if the second husband died, would necessarily put a check upon frivolous divorces, the impossibility of reunion acting as the restraint that a prohibition could not. Clarke supplies the document itself, printing from Maimonides and Bartolocci a full specimen of the bill, with its dating from the creation of the world and its clauses for any other name the parties might bear.

Whether the woman is thereby defiled is the last dispute, and Clarke and Wesley take opposite sides. Clarke reads it absolutely: God counted all such after-marriages pollution, which is the ground on which our Lord argues that whoever marries the woman put away commits adultery; this could not stand if the divorce had been a legal separation, since nothing but adultery can be a legal cause of separation on either side, the wife having as much right to put away her husband as the husband her wife. Wesley denies the absolute sense, that she is not defiled as though her second marriage were a sin, but only with respect to her first husband, to whom she is now among forbidden things, called unclean because they may no more be touched than an unclean thing. Gill notes that the prohibition held even where she had only been espoused to the second man, and gives the purpose plainly, that the rule punished the husband's fickleness and made men cautious how they put their wives away.
5:
The year's exemption is read as a defence of the marriage, not a favour to the man. Henry notes that it fitly follows the laws of divorce, since divorce would be prevented if affection were settled at first; everything should be avoided which might make husband and wife strange to one another, for where the love is wanting there is an inlet to abundance of guilt and grief. Calvin states the danger from both sides, that the bride may fall in love with another before she has grown accustomed to her husband, and that in war many things tempt men to sin; and he adds a remark none of the others would have made, that God's permitting a bride to enjoy herself with her husband is no trifling proof of his indulgence, since the connection cannot but be affected with some sin, which God not only pardons but covers with the veil of holy matrimony. Clarke supplies a parallel from outside Israel, that Alexander ordered the soldiers who had married that year to winter with their wives. Ellicott presses the words, that no warfare shall pass upon him in any form. Gill records a disagreement about who the new wife is, a widow according to Jarchi and a virgin according to the Targum of Jonathan.

Gill notes that the dual number takes in both stones, since if either was taken the other became useless; Clarke explains the domestic fact behind it, that the day's meal was ground each day with no stock kept beforehand, so that to take either stone would leave a family without bread. Calvin generalises, that by the two stones God designates every instrument a workman cannot do without, so that he who takes what supports a poor man's life is as cruel as if he took bread from a starving man. Wesley adds that such taking offends against charity and prudence alike, since by those very things the debtor is enabled both to subsist and to pay. Ellicott contributes the structural note, that the word rendered a man's life is literally a soul, and joins the law of the millstone to the law of manstealing that follows.

That law is given the weight of murder. Calvin says the same punishment is deservedly denounced against the manstealer as against the murderer, since the condition of slaves was so wretched that liberty was more than half of life; and not the stealing only is condemned but the fraud of selling. Gill fixes the terms from the rabbis, that brethren covers Israelite and proselyte and freed servant alike, and that found requires full proof by witnesses.

The command about leprosy is where they openly disagree about what is being commanded. Keil rejects the received reading, that when signs appeared they were to do whatever the priests directed, on two grounds: that the appeal to Miriam does not fit, since she brought leprosy on herself by rebelling against Moses rather than by opposing the priests, and that the reading will not square with the Hebrew construction. Ellicott takes the point to be social rather than procedural, that Miriam, though a leader of Israel, was shut out of the camp seven days, so that no relaxation could be allowed for great or wealthy persons. Calvin surveys the field before entering it, remarking how variously interpreters twist what Moses wrote on leprosy, some being too devoted to allegories and others supposing that God merely gave a sanitary commandment against contagion, a notion he calls poor and almost unmeaning and holds refuted by the reason given for putting lepers outside the camp, that they should not defile the camp in which God dwelt. Gill draws the warning the others do not, that Miriam is remembered to guard against evil suspicions of those in authority, and that none should think it hard to be shut up when the sister of Moses was so used.
10:
Why the creditor must wait outside is answered with unusual force. Calvin imagines what the other rule would license: the creditor ransacking his brother's house and furniture to pick out the pledge at his pleasure, and the avaricious rich, given that option, satisfied with no moderation but seizing on whatever was best, as though making an assault upon the very entrails of the poor, or else contemptuously refusing this and that until they had filled the wretched with rebuke and shame. God therefore will have no pledge reclaimed except what the debtor of his own accord and at his own convenience brings out to him. Wesley names two motives rather than one, that the rule spares the poor man the reproach of having his wants exposed and spares the creditor the greediness which the sight of something he desired and the debtor could not spare would have stirred in him; and on the following verse he adds that the choice of pledge is the borrower's, provided what he brings is sufficient for the purpose. Gill fills in the picture, that the lender stands without doors in the street while the borrower looks out what he can best spare.

The garment returned at sundown raises an obvious objection, and two of the voices meet it from opposite directions. Keil gives the fact that makes the law necessary, that the poor man very often had nothing to pledge but the upper garment in which he slept. Clarke turns that into a question: did the law not preclude pledging altogether, at least in the case of the abjectly poor, for who would take a pledge in the morning which he knew he must restore at night if it were not redeemed? His own answer is that the creditor might resume his claim each morning and have the pledge returned each evening, keeping up his property in it until the debt was discharged. Gill reports the answer the Jews themselves gave to the same question, and it is quite different: the profit of the pledge was that by this means the debt was not released in the seventh year, when all other debts were released, and that the borrower could not dispose of the goods to his children, payment being made from the pledge after his death. Gill also observes that the hour of return followed the kind of pledge, a night covering being restored at sunset and day clothes in the morning, so that the thing went back and forth daily.

What the lender gains by obedience is put in two ways. Wesley takes the blessing literally as the poor man's prayer, and adds a distinction that is his own: though the man's prayers, if he be not himself good, shall not avail for his own behalf, they shall nevertheless avail for the benefit of the one who returned his cloak. On the closing clause he says the act shall be esteemed and accepted by God as a work of righteousness, or of mercy. Keil takes the same clause as a formula used elsewhere in the book and lets it stand without expansion. Calvin, having begun with what the rich would do if unrestrained, ends with what the rule protects, that a man is not to be so stripped as to suffer from cold, and that the creditor is not to take back at all any pledge he knows to be necessary to the poor, whether it be the bed the man sleeps on, or his coverlet, or his cloak.
14:
Calvin ties the two halves together, that the prohibition against oppressing and the command to pay are to be read in connection, so that if a hireling suffers want because we have not paid what he earned, our delay alone convicts us of unrighteousness. Henry widens the oppression beyond wages, to overloading with work, undue rebukes, and withholding proper maintenance, and grounds the whole in memory: a servant, though a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, must not be abused, because thou wast a bondman thyself and knowest what it is to be oppressed by a taskmaster; masters should not be tyrants to their servants, for their Master is in heaven. Gill cites the Jerusalem Targum that the hire is not to be detained by force, adding that neither may it be detained by fraud. Wesley says only that the time appointed governs, whether weekly or daily.

The clause about setting the heart on the wages is rendered several ways. Keil takes it as a longing, that the man lifts up his soul to his hire, gathering the idiom from the Psalms and Jeremiah. Calvin's own version has the man sustaining his life by the wage, with the alternatives set beside it, that he lifteth his soul unto it, that he pants for it, and that he hopes for it for the maintenance of his life. Clarke fills the phrase with observation rather than philology: how natural this is, he says, since the poor servant who seldom sees money yet finds from his master's affluence that money procures every comfort of life, and so longs for the day of payment; and if the pay is delayed he may naturally be expected to cry to God against the man who withholds it.

On fathers and children the commentators agree about the rule and divide about its limits. Keil states the scope, that neither was to suffer death along with the other for crimes in which he had no share, and adds that the command was needed to prevent an abusive transfer into human courts of what belongs to divine justice, the practice being common among the Persians and Macedonians. Calvin makes it a matter of regard for human life, that on one man's crime a whole race was often severely dealt with, so that God interposes for the innocent; natural common sense, he says, dictates that it is an act of barbarous madness to put children to death out of hatred to their father. He then raises the obvious objection himself, that God is said to avenge iniquity to the third and fourth generation, and answers that God is a law unto himself and does not rush by blind impulse to vengeance so as to confound the innocent with the reprobate, but tempers extreme severity with the greatest equity.

Wesley answers the same objection differently, and the difference matters. He grants that God visits the fathers' sins upon the children but denies that he suffers men to do so, and then admits a class of exceptions Calvin does not name: cases where the sovereign Lord of life and death, before whom none is innocent, has himself commanded it, and he instances the herem of the thirteenth chapter and the destruction of Achan's household. Ellicott handles that last case the opposite way, treating Achan, who perished not alone in his iniquity, as falling under a different head rather than as an exception to this rule; and he supplies the history of the precept's observance, that Amaziah the son of Joash is specially noted in Kings and Chronicles for keeping it, and that the Persians did not keep it with Daniel's accusers. Clarke, brief where the others expand, refers the whole question to the eighteenth chapter of Ezekiel, and Gill fixes only that the death in view is judicial, inflicted by the civil magistrate for capital crimes.
17:
Gill puts the charge to judges plainly, that the stranger and the fatherless are unable to defend themselves and have few if any to take their part, so that magistrates must take particular care to do them justice or God will require it of them. Keil groups the section and observes that the ground given at its end is the same as at its beginning, the memory of bondage in Egypt. Wesley alone qualifies the clause about the widow's raiment, holding that what may not be pledged is the clothing she has daily and necessary use of, as being poor, and that the rule does not concern rich persons or superfluous raiment.

On the memory of Egypt the voices take different roads. Gill takes it as a producer of fellow-feeling, that the remembrance may cause sympathy with persons in distress, and particularly with the stranger and the fatherless and the widow. Clarke turns it into a warning about wealth, and the observation is his own: most people who have affluence rose from comparative penury, since those born to estates frequently squander them, and such men ought to remember what their feelings and fears and anxieties were when they were poor and abject; want of attention to this most wholesome precept, he says, is why pride and arrogance are the general characteristics of those who have risen from poverty to affluence, and it is their conduct which gave rise to the rugged proverb that if you set a beggar on horseback he will ride to the devil.

The gleaning laws produce the sharpest disagreement in the passage, and it concerns whose the leavings are. Clarke states the case in terms of ownership: this is an addition to the law given in Leviticus, and the corners of the field, the gleanings and the forgotten sheaf were all the property of the poor, a principle the Hebrews extended to any part of the produce forgotten at the general ingathering. Calvin will not go so far, and hedges the duty on both sides. He grounds it warmly enough, that when God's bounty is exercised before our eyes it invites us to imitate him, and that it is a sign of ingratitude to withhold unkindly and maliciously what we derive from his blessing. But he denies that God requires those who have abundance to give away their produce so profusely as to despoil themselves by enriching others, citing Paul's measure that the relief of the poor should not bring the distributing rich into distress; God permits every man to reap his corn and gather his vintage and enjoy his abundance, provided only that the rich do not grudge the poor the gleaning of the grapes and the corn. And he limits the other side as expressly, that God does not absolutely assign to the poor whatever remains, as though they might seize it as their own, but reserves some small portion for them. Between Clarke's property of the poor and Calvin's portion reserved but not assigned there is a real difference about what the poor may claim.

The agricultural detail is Gill's, that the olive was beaten with sticks and staves to bring down the ripe fruit, and that the grapes were gathered at much the same season, both after the wheat harvest about the end of June, those countries being more forward. Keil sets the three commands side by side without comment, each ending with the same three beneficiaries. Gill closes the chapter on the closing formula, that the Israelites in Egypt would have been glad to enjoy favours as small as these, even to glean in another man's field, and that this is why the thing is commanded them.
